a: If you go anyway, then act! Be strong for battle!
p: The Hebrew seems ironic: go and be strong, God will still trip you. The Greek reads differently.

readings.orig: כִּי אִם־בֹּא אַתָּה עֲשֵׂה חֲזַק לַמִּלְחָמָה
readings.en: For if you go, act, be strong for battle
readings.plain: If you go anyway, then act! Be strong for battle!

readings.orig: ὅτι ἐὰν ὑπολάβῃς κατισχῦσαι ἐν τούτοις
readings.en: For if you think to prevail with these
readings.plain: If you think you will be strong with these

why: The Hebrew makes sense as irony and is the harder reading. The Greek probably paraphrased a difficult text.

t: City of Judah or City of David?
p: Chronicles' Hebrew says Amaziah was buried 'in the city of Judah'. Kings and the Greek say 'the City of David'.

readings.w: 2 Kings 14:20; Septuagint of Chronicles (Rahlfs: ἐν πόλει Δαυιδ); some Hebrew manuscripts

why: "City of Judah" may be a slip, but it could also be an old name for Jerusalem: the Babylonian Chronicle calls Jerusalem "the city of Judah" (al Yahudu). The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.

p: Chronicles' Hebrew spells the port Eloth. Kings and the Greek have Elath.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of 2 Chronicles (also 2 Chronicles 8:17)

why: Two forms of one name for the same town at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba. The Plain English Translation prints each book's own form.

p: The written text spells the queen mother's name Jechiliah; the margin reads Jecoliah, as in Kings.

readings.w: Qere (margin of the Masoretic Text); 2 Kings 15:2
Ketiv (written text of the Masoretic Text)

why: The margin matches Kings; the site's 2 Kings Plain English Translation has Jecoliah.

a: a man who understood the visions of God
p: Most Hebrew manuscripts say Zechariah taught 'in the visions of God'. Others, and the Greek, say 'in the fear of God'.

readings.en: who understood the seeing of God
readings.plain: a man who understood the visions of God

readings.w: Many Hebrew manuscripts; Septuagint (Rahlfs: τοῦ συνίοντος ἐν φόβῳ κυρίου); Syriac; many modern versions
readings.en: who understood the fear of God
readings.plain: a man who understood the fear of God

why: The two readings differ by one letter. "Fear of God" is the more common phrase, which may be why copyists preferred it; the Plain English Translation keeps the rarer Leningrad reading, though either may be original.

p: The Hebrew says the Ammonites paid tribute. The Greek has Minaeans, which suits the context better.

readings.w: Septuagint (Rahlfs) (καὶ ἔδωκαν οἱ Μιναῖοι δῶρα); many modern scholars

why: The Greek matches the Meunites of 26:7 and the southward direction of the verse, and many scholars prefer it. But Ammon also paid tribute to Jotham (27:5), and the Hebrew makes sense, so the Plain English Translation keeps it.

p: A spelling difference between the written text and the margin.
why: The margin gives the common form of the name. The same holds for Jeiel in 29:13 and Jehiel in 29:14.

a: He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem sixteen years.
p: This verse repeats 27:1. The main Greek manuscripts leave it out.

readings.en: He was twenty-five years old when he became king...
readings.plain: He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem sixteen years.

why: The repetition may be a copyist's error, or a deliberate frame around Jotham's reign. Chronicles repeats a summary elsewhere too (compare 2 Kings 8:17 and 2 Chronicles 21:5, 21:20). The Plain English Translation keeps it.

a: he burned his sons in the fire
p: Chronicles' Hebrew says 'burned'. Kings and the Greek of Chronicles say 'made pass through' the fire.

readings.en: he burned his sons in the fire
readings.plain: he burned his sons in the fire

readings.w: 2 Kings 16:3 (singular 'son'); Septuagint of Chronicles (Rahlfs: καὶ διῆγεν τὰ τέκνα αὐτοῦ διὰ πυρός); Syriac; Targum
readings.en: he made his children pass through the fire
readings.plain: he made his sons pass through the fire

why: The verbs differ by one letter (b'r and 'br). It could be a copying slip or a deliberate sharpening by the Chronicler. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew of Chronicles; see the note.

p: The Hebrew has the plural 'kings of Assyria'. The Greek, Syriac and Kings have the singular.

readings.w: Septuagint (Rahlfs: πρὸς βασιλέα Ασσουρ); Syriac; Vulgate; 2 Kings 16:7

why: The plural may be a general expression (compare 30:6; 32:4) or a slip. The Plain English Translation keeps it; the meaning is Tiglath-pileser.

p: The Hebrew calls Ahaz 'king of Israel'. The Greek and some Hebrew manuscripts say 'king of Judah'.

readings.w: Some Hebrew manuscripts; Septuagint (Rahlfs: δι᾽ Αχαζ βασιλέα Ιουδα); Vulgate

why: Chronicles often calls Judah "Israel" (21:2; 28:27), and the harder reading is more likely original. The ancient versions smoothed it.

p: The Hebrew says Ahaz was buried 'in the city, in Jerusalem'. The Greek says 'the city of David'.

readings.en: he was buried in the city of David

why: The Greek brings Chronicles into line with Kings. The Hebrew of Chronicles distinguishes the city from the royal tombs.

p: The written text and the margin spell the word for 'terror' differently.
why: Two spellings of the same word, used in Jeremiah 15:4 and 24:9. The meaning does not change.

t: The Levite priests, or priests and Levites?
p: The Hebrew and the Greek read 'the priests the Levites'. Many Hebrew manuscripts and some versions add 'and'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint (Rahlfs: οἱ ἱερεῖς οἱ Λευῖται)
Many Hebrew manuscripts; Syriac; Vulgate (as reported by Allen and the BHS apparatus)

why: "The Levite priests" is Deuteronomy's phrase (Deuteronomy 18:1) and fits the priestly blessing; the Greek supports it. "And" was easily added under the influence of 30:25.

p: A spelling difference between the written text and the margin.
why: Spelling only; the same in 31:13 and 35:9.

a: He guided them on every side
p: The Hebrew says God 'guided' them. The Greek and Vulgate say he 'gave them rest', a phrase common in Chronicles.

readings.en: and he guided them on every side
readings.plain: He guided them on every side

readings.w: Septuagint (Rahlfs: καὶ κατέπαυσεν αὐτοὺς κυκλόθεν); Vulgate; many modern versions
readings.orig: καὶ κατέπαυσεν αὐτοὺς κυκλόθεν (Hebrew behind it, reconstructed: וַיָּנַח לָהֶם)
readings.en: and he gave them rest on every side
readings.plain: He gave them rest on every side

why: "Rest on every side" is a set phrase in Chronicles (14:7; 15:15; 20:30), which makes it attractive but also explains why a copyist might have produced it. The Hebrew makes sense, so the Plain English Translation keeps it.

a: in the scroll of the kings of Judah and Israel
p: The Hebrew says the vision of Isaiah is 'in' the book of the kings. The Greek has 'and in the book', two sources.

readings.en: in (or upon) the scroll of the kings of Judah and Israel
readings.plain: in the scroll of the kings of Judah and Israel

readings.orig: καὶ ἐπὶ βιβλίου βασιλέων Ιουδα καὶ Ισραηλ
readings.en: and in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel
readings.plain: and in the scroll of the kings of Judah and Israel

why: The Hebrew probably means the Isaiah material was included in the royal scroll, as Isaiah 36–39 is in 2 Kings 18–20.

p: The written text says Manasseh 'set up' the altar; the margin reads 'rebuilt'.
why: The two words differ by one letter. Both make sense; the Plain English Translation follows the margin.

p: The Hebrew names an unknown Hozai. The Greek reads 'the seers'.
why: Hozai may be a name otherwise unknown, or a slip for "the visionaries" of 33:18. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew; see the note.

a: they buried him at his house
t: At his house, or in the garden?
p: The Hebrew says Manasseh was buried 'at his house'. The Greek, with Kings, says 'in the garden of his house'.

readings.plain: they buried him at his house

readings.orig: ἔθαψαν αὐτὸν ἐν παραδείσῳ οἴκου αὐτοῦ
readings.en: they buried him in the garden of his house
readings.plain: they buried him in the garden of his house

why: The Greek may have restored a word from Kings; Chronicles may have shortened Kings. The meaning is close.

a: and in the ruined places around them
p: The written text has two words; the margin one. The meaning is disputed.

readings.w: Qere (margin), consonants revocalized as 'ruins'; most modern versions
readings.plain: and in the ruined places around them

readings.w: Qere as pointed in the Masoretic Text; KJV

readings.en: in the hill country (?) of their houses
readings.plain: in the hills of their houses

readings.en: and in their places round about
readings.plain: and in their places round about

why: "Ruins" fits the devastated north and needs only a change of vowels. The KJV's "with their mattocks" follows the Masoretic pointing.

t: People of Jerusalem, or they returned?
p: The written text says the silver came from 'the people of Jerusalem'. The margin reads 'they returned to Jerusalem'.

readings.w: Ketiv (written text); Septuagint (Rahlfs: καὶ οἰκούντων ἐν Ιερουσαλημ); many modern versions

readings.plain: and they went back to Jerusalem

why: The written text completes the list of givers and agrees with the Greek; the margin's "they returned" is less natural here. This is one of the few places the Plain English Translation prefers the Ketiv.

a: Shallum son of Tokhath, son of Hasrah
p: Kings has 'Shallum son of Tikvah, son of Harhas'. Chronicles has Tokhath and Hasrah.

readings.en: Shallum son of Tokhath, son of Hasrah
readings.plain: Shallum son of Tokhath, son of Hasrah
Shallum son of Tokehath, son of Hasrah

readings.en: Shallum son of Tikvah, son of Harhas
readings.plain: Shallum son of Tikvah, son of Harhas

readings.en: Sellem son of Thakouath, son of Chelles
readings.plain: Shallum son of Thakouath, son of Chelles

why: The names in the two books differ by letters easily confused or transposed in Hebrew (q/qw, rch/sr). These are copying differences, not a deliberate change. The Plain English Translation keeps each book's own form.

p: The written text and the margin spell the word for 'teachers' differently.
why: The margin gives the usual participle. The sense is much the same; compare Nehemiah 8:7, where Levites teach the people.

a: It was in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign that this Passover was held.
t: Extra verses in the Greek and in 1 Esdras
p: After this verse the Greek adds 35:19a–d, drawn from 2 Kings 23:24–27. 1 Esdras has a shorter addition of its own.

readings.plain: It was in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign that this Passover was held.

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus, as translated by Brenton): adds 35:19a–d (not printed in the blueletterbible.org Rahlfs page; Rahlfs 35:19 itself reads τῷ ὀκτωκαιδεκάτῳ ἔτει τῆς βασιλείας Ιωσια)
readings.en: Adds that Josiah removed the mediums, teraphim and idols to fulfill the law; that there was no king like him; that the LORD did not turn from his anger because of Manasseh's provocations; and that the LORD said he would remove Judah as he removed Israel and reject Jerusalem
readings.plain: It was in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign that this Passover was held. [Plus four verses like 2 Kings 23:24–27]

readings.en: Adds that Josiah's works were upright before the Lord with a heart full of godliness, and that the sins of earlier times grieved the Lord
readings.plain: It was in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign that this Passover was held. [Plus a short note on Josiah's godliness and the earlier sins]

why: The Greek supplies material from Kings that Chronicles had left out, including the blame on Manasseh that Chronicles avoids. 1 Esdras has a different, shorter addition. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: to make war at Carchemish on the Euphrates
p: The Hebrew names Carchemish. The Greek of Chronicles says Neco went against the king of Assyria, at the Euphrates.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 1 Esdras 1:25, KJV numbering ('Carchamis upon Euphrates')
readings.en: to fight at Carchemish on the Euphrates
readings.plain: to make war at Carchemish on the Euphrates

readings.orig: ἐπὶ τὸν βασιλέα Ἀσσυρίων ἐπὶ τὸν ποταμὸν Εὐφράτην
readings.en: against the king of the Assyrians, to the river Euphrates
readings.plain: to make war against the king of Assyria at the Euphrates

why: The Greek reflects Kings' "to the king of Assyria" (2 Kings 23:29), with a preposition that makes Neco Assyria's enemy. In fact he came as Assyria's ally. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew of Chronicles.

a: He disguised himself to fight him
p: The Hebrew says Josiah disguised himself, like Ahab. The Greek says he 'strengthened himself' to fight.

readings.plain: He disguised himself to fight him

readings.w: Septuagint (Rahlfs); compare 1 Esdras 1:28, KJV numbering ('undertook to fight')
readings.plain: He was determined to fight him

why: The Hebrew links Josiah's death with Ahab's (1 Kings 22:30) and is likely original. The Greek may have read a similar-looking verb or avoided the comparison.

p: Chronicles says God spoke through Neco. 1 Esdras says Josiah ignored the prophet Jeremiah.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint of Chronicles (Rahlfs: τῶν λόγων Νεχαω διὰ στόματος θεοῦ)
readings.en: the words of Neco from the mouth of God
the words of the prophet Jeremy, spoken by the mouth of the Lord
readings.plain: the words of the prophet Jeremiah from the LORD's mouth

why: 1 Esdras seems to soften the idea that a pharaoh spoke for God. The Hebrew of Chronicles is the harder reading and is followed.

a: he reigned three months in Jerusalem
t: Three added verses in the Greek
p: After this verse the Greek adds 36:2a–c, from 2 Kings 23:31–33: Jehoahaz's mother, his evil, and his arrest.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 1 Esdras 1:34–35 (KJV numbering)
readings.plain: he reigned three months in Jerusalem

readings.orig: καὶ ὄνομα τῆς μητρὸς αὐτοῦ Αμιταλ θυγάτηρ Ιερεμιου ἐκ Λοβενα ... καὶ ἔδησεν αὐτὸν Φαραω Νεχαω ἐν Δεβλαθα ἐν γῇ Εμαθ
readings.en: His mother's name was Amital daughter of Jeremiah, from Lobena. He did evil before the Lord as his fathers had done. Pharaoh Neco bound him at Deblatha in the land of Hamath, so that he would not reign in Jerusalem
readings.plain: he reigned three months in Jerusalem. [Plus: his mother Amital (Hamutal) of Libnah; he did evil; Neco bound him at Riblah]

why: The Greek fills Chronicles from 2 Kings 23:31–33, with Riblah spelled Deblatha. The Hebrew of Chronicles is followed.

a: Joahaz his brother, Neco took away and brought to Egypt.
p: The Greek adds that Jehoahaz died in Egypt, then a verse (36:4a) on the tax Jehoiakim raised for Neco.

readings.plain: Joahaz his brother, Neco took away and brought to Egypt.

readings.orig: καὶ ἀπέθανεν ἐκεῖ ... τότε ἤρξατο ἡ γῆ φορολογεῖσθαι τοῦ δοῦναι τὸ ἀργύριον ἐπὶ στόμα Φαραω
readings.en: and he died there. They gave the silver and gold to Pharaoh; then the land began to be taxed, to pay the silver at Pharaoh's word, each man by his means
readings.plain: Joahaz his brother, Neco took away and brought to Egypt, and he died there. [Plus: the land taxed to pay Pharaoh]

why: Both additions match 2 Kings 23:34–35. The Hebrew of Chronicles is followed.

a: He did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD his God
t: Four added verses in the Greek
p: The Greek names Jehoiakim's mother and then adds 36:5a–d, drawn from 2 Kings 24:1–4.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 1 Esdras 1:39 (KJV numbering)
readings.plain: He did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD his God

readings.orig: καὶ ὄνομα τῆς μητρὸς αὐτοῦ Ζεχωρα θυγάτηρ Νηριου ἐκ Ραμα ... διὰ τὰς ἁμαρτίας Μανασση
readings.en: Jehoiakim's mother was Zechora daughter of Nerias, from Rama. He served Nebuchadnezzar three years and rebelled; the Lord sent Chaldeans and raiders from Syria, Moab, Ammon and Samaria; the Lord's anger was on Judah for Manasseh's sins and for the innocent blood Jehoiakim shed
readings.plain: He did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD his God [plus additions like 2 Kings 24:1–4]

why: As at 35:19, 36:2 and 36:4, the Greek fills Chronicles from Kings, though its mother's name (Zechora daughter of Nerias, from Rama) differs from Kings' Zebudah daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah (2 Kings 23:36). The Hebrew of Chronicles is followed.

a: the abhorrent things he did and what was found against him
p: The Hebrew speaks of Jehoiakim's abhorrent deeds. The Greek has 'all that he did' and adds a burial in 'Ganoza'.

readings.en: his abominations that he did and what was found against him
readings.plain: the abhorrent things he did and what was found against him

readings.orig: καὶ πάντα ἃ ἐποίησεν ... καὶ ἐκοιμήθη Ιωακιμ μετὰ τῶν πατέρων αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐτάφη ἐν Γανοζα μετὰ τῶν πατέρων αὐτοῦ
readings.en: all that he did ... and Jehoiakim lay down with his ancestors and was buried in Ganoza with his ancestors
readings.plain: all that he did. He lay down with his ancestors and was buried in Ganoza with his ancestors

why: The Greek has a burial notice in place of the charge. Ganoza is a transliteration, probably of gan 'uzza', "the garden of Uzza," where Manasseh and Amon were buried (2 Kings 21:18; 2 Kings 21:26). The Hebrew is followed.

p: Chronicles' Hebrew says Jehoiachin was eight. Kings, Rahlfs' Greek and 1 Esdras say eighteen.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Codex Vaticanus (Brenton: 'eight')
2 Kings 24:8; Septuagint (Rahlfs, with Alexandrinus and the Lucianic manuscripts); Syriac; 1 Esdras 1:43 (KJV numbering; 1:41 in Rahlfs); some Hebrew manuscripts

why: Eighteen is almost certainly the original number, since Jehoiachin had wives (2 Kings 24:15); "ten" probably fell out of the Hebrew in copying. The Plain English Translation still prints the Hebrew of Chronicles, as this part does for every number, and flags the slip here and in the note. The book owner may prefer to print eighteen, with the Masoretic Text as the variant.

p: The Hebrew calls Zedekiah Jehoiachin's brother. The Greek and Kings make him his uncle.
why: "Brother" can mean relative, and the Greek may have clarified it. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew; the note explains.

p: Ezra 1:1, repeating this verse, has 'from the mouth' (mippi). Chronicles and 1 Esdras have 'by the mouth'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of 2 Chronicles; Septuagint (Rahlfs: διὰ στόματος Ιερεμιου); 1 Esdras 2:1 (ἐν στόματι Ιερεμιου)

why: A small difference between the two copies of the decree. Chronicles matches its own phrase in 36:21, and 1 Esdras sides with it.
